text: This is doeff: algebraic effects for Python.
Your code says what it wants. Handlers, stacked around it, decide how it happens.
A doeff program is a Python generator, marked with at-do.
yield Fetch fetches nothing by itself. It hands a request, called an effect, outward.
A handler answers it. The answer comes back as page, and the code goes on.
Here is monitor. It only says what it wants: a page, a line, and a thirty-minute wait.
Each yield hands an effect outward. The code never says how it is done.
Handlers wrap the program in layers. You choose the stack when you run it.
An effect travels outward until a layer that handles it catches it.
Delay reaches the virtual clock. What does that layer get?
Along with the effect, the handler also gets k: the rest of your program.
Holding k, it decides when the rest runs: now, later, at nine thirty, or never.
The virtual clock sets the time to nine thirty and resumes k at once. No real wait.
A scheduler is a layer too. Spawn starts two monitors at once.
Each Delay parks its k. The virtual clock keeps them in wake-up order.
No task is ready, so the clock jumps to nine ten, and b's k runs.
Then nine thirty for a. The same four lines, in the same order, every run.
Now swap the stack, and keep the code.
Test handlers on the left. Production handlers on the right.
yield Fetch: the program asks for the page.
yield Log: it writes a line.
yield Delay, thirty minutes: each clock decides what waiting means.
Test skips the wait. Production really waits, shown in fast-forward.
Test is done. Production is still waiting out the thirty minutes.
The wait is over. Production checks again.
Same code, same output. Test: a few milliseconds. Production: thirty real minutes.
doeff: algebraic effects for Python. Stack the layers you need around the same code. pip install doeff.
